Title: The Spread Eagle Starts With a Pivot, Not a Stretch
Description: Both skates open, toes pointing opposite ways, rolling as though they were on a rail. It looks like a position you pull your feet into, and it is not. Come out of a small lemon with the skates parallel, press down on the front of one skate, and let its heel swing all the way round through half a turn. Knees bent, weight in the wheels. The slight curve your line takes is normal and correct. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: A Straight Eagle Is a Hip Problem, Not a Skating One
Description: Your spread eagle curves. Everybody's does, and the curved version is the normal one. Holding a dead straight line is a different question entirely: it needs external rotation at the hips that not every body has, and it is not something skating practice will hand you. It is trained off your skates like any other range of motion. Stop rebuilding your technique to fix something your hips are doing. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: One Side Trained Is Half a Move Learnt
Description: Every skater has a side that arrives on its own and a side that feels like week one all over again. Practise only the good one and you have not learnt the move, you have learnt half of it — and the day the ground picks the direction for you, half is what you will have. Alternate left and right inside the same session, deliberately, badly. Working both sides is also what builds the thighs and the adductors evenly. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Title: Shoot the Duck Is Muscle, Not Technique
Description: The squat with one leg stretched out in front has no trick hiding inside it. There is no cue you are missing — it is quadriceps, and the way in is repetition. French skaters have never even agreed on a name for it: théière, cafetière, pistolet, bonne femme, four names for one move and no winner. What they do agree on is that the people who can hold it are the people who have squatted a few hundred times. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Six Wheels on the Floor Before Four
Description: The progression has four steps and everyone jumps to the last one. Squat on the spot first, skates hip width, arms out in front, on a beat. Then, still squatting, stretch one leg out while keeping all six wheels on the floor — four under you, two under the extended foot — and pull it back, using an arm to help. That six to four crossing is the step that decides whether you get the move. Only then, one foot, then rolling. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Arabesque Straightens From the Hip, Not the Leg
Description: The leg behind you will not straighten by being lifted. It straightens when your hip travels backwards, as though you were about to sit down on something behind you, and you should feel that pull in the hamstring of the standing leg. Without the hip going back, the free leg stays bent however hard you raise it. Move your weight across through your navel first, then stack head, hip and skate over the standing leg. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Your Shoulder Blades Hold the Arabesque Up
Description: Everything above the waist decides whether the shape stays over the skate. Draw the shoulder blades together, open the chest, keep the upper body switched on — a soft back folds forward and takes the whole position down with it. And place your arms from the very first attempt instead of adding them once the leg works: they are not decoration on top of the figure, they are where the balance actually sits. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Forty-Five Degrees Is Already a Real Arabesque
Description: Height is optional, and that is the part nobody tells you. A free leg at forty-five degrees is a genuine arabesque. Ninety is better. Anything past ninety is for your own pleasure and adds nothing to the figure. The order matters more than the angle: balance first, flexibility second, because a low arabesque held still beats a high one you fall out of. Nearly anyone can hold the low version. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Downtown Is Eight Counts, Two of Them Standing Still
Description: Cross in front, cross behind, stop. One, the skates open. Two, one crosses in front. Three, they open into a spread eagle. Four, the other crosses behind. Five, uncross. Six, bring them back alongside. Seven and eight, you do not move at all. Those last two counts are part of the step and not a gap in it — the dancers who look unhurried are the ones who genuinely stop. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Spread Eagle Is the Hinge of the Downtown
Description: Count three of the downtown is a spread eagle, and it is not there for decoration. It is the balance point the whole step turns on: the front cross arrives into it and the back cross leaves from it, so a shaky eagle leaves both crosses with nothing to hang on. Shift your weight fully onto the leg that stays down before the back cross goes anywhere. Learn the eagle on its own first, then learn the step. Quad technique, from Najete Kada.
